# third_party/PINCache

[PINCache](https://github.com/pinterest/PINCache), Pinterest's disk and memory cache for Objective-C. Vibe caches metadata and waveform data in it. Other authors' code: **do not restyle it.** It depends on `third_party/PINOperation`. Its template is `VibeLibsPINCache`, which lists `VibeLibsPINOperation`.

## Building

Its files import each other as `<PINCache/...>` and `<PINOperation/...>`, so the template searches `third_party/` itself. It also searches this directory, for an app that imports `"PINCache.h"`. Its sources build with the static analyzer off and `-Wno-documentation-html`. `PINDiskCache.m` builds with `-fobjc-arc-exceptions` instead, as the pod's ARC-exception-safe subspec did. `LICENSE.txt` and `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` stay out of an app's bundle.

## Fixes of our own

**`PINDiskCache.m` is modified.** Each change is marked `Vibe:`, so `grep -rn 'Vibe:' third_party/PINCache third_party/PINOperation` lists them for re-applying after an update.

- The access-count xattr is neither written per hit nor read per file at launch, unless eviction is least-frequently-used.
- A hit re-dates its file, and the date the eviction sorts by, only once that date is a day old.
- Outside a TTL cache, a write removes no age-limit xattr, since none is ever set.
- A hit reads its file outside the cache's one lock, as it already deserialized. So concurrent hits run concurrently.
- An automatic trim cuts to 90% of the byte limit. So a full cache sorts its entries once per tenth of the limit written, not on every write.
- `recordsOnDemand` keeps no record of the entries in memory, reading each from its file. A sweep lists the directory a thousand files to a pool, once the disk state is known, outside the lock, and none runs that has nothing to do: a size trim under its target, or an age trim with no entry made before its date, which lists only those. It is one way, set before the first write and the limits, and for a least-recently-used cache that is not a TTL cache: it asserts, and refuses any other. `files/DiskCache`'s AGENTS.md has what it saves and costs.
- With `recordsOnDemand`, a hit takes no lock: it opens the file once and takes its dates from that file, with no second stat. Only a re-date, once a day, first asks whether the file is still there. A trim sorts its listing before it takes the lock, which it then holds only to read the byte count and choose the entries, and each removal takes it again. An enumeration holds no lock while its block runs, so a usage count no longer stalls writes and removals. A trim removes a listed entry only while its file has the listing's creation date, so an entry written again since stays. A file that won't decode is removed as any entry is, so the byte count follows, and only while it is the file the hit read.
- The launch's count enumerates the directory a thousand files to a pool, with no lock held for the listing, not into one array under the lock, which held about 160 MB of URLs at 200,000 entries. It adds each file to the byte count as it counts it, rather than setting the count at its end, which lost the bytes of a write made meanwhile.
- With `recordsOnDemand`, a write, a removal, and a move never wait for the launch's count. Each first settles every key it changes: unless the count or an earlier change already accounted for the key's file, it adds that file's bytes, and its creation date to the age limit's bound. The count then skips the file, since its listed size may be older than the change. A set of 64-bit hashes of the file names records what is accounted for, freed when the count ends. It stays at most half full, so its slots take 4 MB up to 262,144 files, which a full store of 4 KB files reaches, and 8 MB past that, with both, 12 MB, for a moment while it grows. Two names whose hashes collide, under once in 10^8 launches at that size, leave one file's bytes uncounted until the next launch. If the set can't grow, it stores nothing more, and every later change waits for the count as all once did, while the count counts every file not already settled. The set lives in the cache, so making it can't fail. A removal of everything during the count stops it, since the files it would list are gone. Known and unchanged: two caches on one folder each keep their own count, so a change through one after the other listed its file leaves the other's total wrong until its next launch. And the count names files as the volume lists them, so two keys that differ only in case would count twice on a case-insensitive volume.
- `VibePINDiskCacheCountSeamFunction`, in `PINDiskCache.h`, is a test seam: each launch count calls it before it lists, before each file, and after the last, so a test can hold the count there. It is NULL in an app.
- Outside a TTL cache, the age limit counts from an entry's last use, its modification date, which a hit moves once a day at most. Upstream's notes say "All access to the cache is dated", and its age trim sorted by the creation date. A TTL cache still ages from the creation date. With `recordsOnDemand`, the bound the age trim reads, `oldestUse`, is the earliest modification date, which a hit only moves later. A trim removes a listed entry only while its file has the listing's modification date too, so a hit since the listing keeps it.
- `byteLimit` and `ageLimit` are set at once, under the lock, and each setter's trim reads the limit as it stands when it runs. Upstream set each in an operation on its concurrent queue, so a later limit could lose to an earlier one, and an earlier, smaller limit's trim could run after a larger one was set. A limit set to the value it has schedules nothing, so an app that sets a store's default again starts no second age trim and timer.
- A wait for a writable disk or a known disk state loops, since a condition's wait can wake for nothing. A trim's loop stops before its count could wrap below zero.
- `moveObjectForKey:toKey:` moves an entry to another key as one `renamex_np` of its file, with `RENAME_EXCL`, under the cache's lock, and moves its record if the cache keeps one. Its bytes, dates, and size go with it, so the byte count stays. It refuses, leaving both keys as they were, when the old key has no entry, the new key has one, or the keys are equal. A hit on the old key that races it misses. The waveform and metadata caches move entries this way after a tag-only rewrite.
- The trims sort with total orders when a record's size or date is nil, as it is when its file's attributes could not be read at launch. A nil size sorts as the largest and a nil date as the oldest, so such entries go first. Before, a nil size raised in the size trim. This is the comparator half of upstream's `0073330`. Its batched selection is not taken: a trim here already lists the whole directory, so the sort's own array is a small share of its memory.
